justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users through wide sidewalks on both sides, a multi-lane carriageway, and a marked pedestrian crossing.
Street lighting, planted verges, and a formal sidewalk edge appear to be provided continuously along the corridor rather than concentrated at one frontage only.
Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free crossing details are clearly visible at the zebra crossing from this viewpoint.
safety: The roadway has clear lane markings, center lines, directional arrows, and a zebra crossing, which improve legibility for drivers and crossing pedestrians.
Tall streetlights are installed continuously along the road, supporting basic traffic and pedestrian safety, especially after dark.
Traffic volumes appear low and sightlines are long and unobstructed, but the wide carriageway can still encourage higher vehicle speeds and lengthen pedestrian exposure at the crossing.
livability: The right side includes trees, shrubs, and landscaped strips, which soften the corridor and provide some everyday environmental quality.
The left side has institutional or office-style buildings with limited visible ground-floor activity, so street life appears relatively weak.
There are no visible benches, kiosks, bus shelters, or active social nodes in the frame, reducing the sense of daily convenience and public sociability.
sustainability: Street trees, planted medians/edges, and continuous landscape beds contribute to urban greening and some ecological value.
The street geometry supports walking through sidewalks and crossing infrastructure, which is more sustainable than a road without pedestrian facilities.
No dedicated bike lane, bus stop, or visible rainwater-management feature is evident, so sustainable mobility and green infrastructure are only partially supported.
aesthetics: The corridor looks clean and well maintained, with fresh pavement, orderly lane markings, and tidy sidewalks.
The street has a coherent visual structure created by evenly spaced streetlights, aligned trees, and a broad open vista.
The combination of modern building facades on the left and landscaped greenery on the right gives the street a balanced and relatively pleasant appearance.
comfort: Physical comfort is supported by broad, even sidewalks and smooth road surfacing with few visible obstructions.
Thermal comfort is mixed because there are street trees and planting, but much of the sidewalk and crossing area remains exposed to direct sun.
Psychological comfort is moderate: the street feels spacious and uncrowded, yet the very wide roadway and sparse human activity can make it feel less intimate for pedestrians.
walkability: Continuous sidewalks on both sides and a visible zebra crossing provide the basic ingredients for walkable movement.
Walkability is weakened by the wide road section, which increases crossing distance and reduces pedestrian priority despite the marked crosswalk.
The route lacks visible pedestrian-scale amenities such as benches, shade structures, active storefronts, or protective curb extensions that would make walking more attractive.
bikeability: There is no clearly marked or protected bicycle lane visible on the carriageway or beside the sidewalk.
Cyclists would likely need to share space with motor vehicles on a relatively wide road where speeds may be higher, reducing perceived safety.
No bicycle parking, bike symbols, colored cycle markings, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible, so cycling support appears minimal.
